fatal_errors: The proposed equiatomic or near-equiatomic single-phase FCC initial state is inconsistent with the target Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy and with the strong tendency of AlCoCrFeNi compositions to form BCC/B2 phases.
The intervention changes Al concentration rather than comparing annealing at 1100, 1200, and 1300 °C followed by water quenching.

The mechanism based on FCC stacking-fault energy and lattice distortion misses the target mechanism of BCC miscibility-gap spinodal decomposition, reciprocal Ni–Al versus Co–Cr–Fe partitioning, and subsequent B2 ordering.
The baseline is the wrong composition and does not represent either the 1100 °C quenched condition or the undecomposed high-temperature BCC structural state.

The cited evidence does not establish that an optimal Al concentration suppresses intermetallic precipitation, radiation-induced segregation, and diffusion while retaining all four claimed performance classes.
explanation: The response addresses the broad motivation of phase stability and multifunctional performance, but it does not reconstruct the studied alloy, controlled temperature/quench comparison, observed reciprocal BCC/B2 hierarchy, or hardness trend. Its composition-series experiment is testable in principle, yet the central assumptions are weak: Al commonly promotes ordered B2 or other precipitates in this alloy family rather than simply stabilizing a moderately distorted single-phase FCC matrix. E1 concerns Al+Ti-induced L12 strengthening and even reports excess-content precipitates; E2 concerns a thermoelectric joining interface; and E3 only supports the role of Al/Cr in oxidation. None validates the asserted stacking-fault-energy, irradiation, or phase-suppression mechanism. The falsification rule is also diffuse because it requires simultaneous failure across several largely independent properties rather than a decisive mechanistic test linking Al, stacking-fault energy, phase stability, and twinning.
